Wildfires in western North America have increased in size and intensity over the past several decades because of climate change and landscape alterations that have affected ignitions and fuels. The EcoGRAPH group has studied the effects of climate, vegetation, and forest management on wildfire in the western United States ([Liu and Wimberly 2015](#western-refs)) and developed models to project the effects of climate change on future fire regimes ([Liu and Wimberly 2016](#western-refs)). These studies projected increased burned area and showed that the indirect effects of shifting vegetation types in response to climate change will be as important as the direct effects of climate change on fire weather and fuel moisture. We also projected the impacts of climate change and wildland-urban interface (WUI) expansion on fire risk in the Colorado Front Range ([Liu et al. 2015](#western-refs)). The combined effects of these two factors were non-linear, with climate change exacerbating the risks from the expansion of low-density homes into fire-prone vegetation types.

Fuel treatments, such as thinning and prescribed burning, are a potentially valuable tool for adapting to changing fire regimes. We used satellite remote sensing data and fire behavior models to analyze the effects of different types of fuel treatments on wildfire size and severity ([Wimberly et al. 2009](#western-refs), [Cochrane et al. 2012](#western-refs)). Treatments that combined the reduction of canopy fuels by thinning with the reduction of surface fuels by prescribed burning or mastication were most effective at reducing fire severities and sizes. We also explored the complex influences of forest roads on fire regimes in dry forests of eastern Washington, USA. Both human and lightning ignitions were more frequent close to roads than in more remote areas ([Narayanaraj and Wimberly, 2012](#western-refs)). However, fires frequently stopped spreading near roads ([Narayanaraj and Wimberly, 2011](#western-refs)), and fire severity also tended to be lower in the vicinity of roads ([Narayanaraj and Wimberly, 2013](#western-refs)).

In the Pacific Northwest region of the United States, old-growth forests are characterized by large tree sizes, accumulations of dead wood, and complex horizontal and vertical structure. The extent of old-growth forests was greatly reduced by logging during the 20th century ([Wimberly and Ohmann 2004](#western-refs)). However, large wildfires occurred in the region prior to European settlement, raising the question of how current levels of old growth compare to those under pre-settlement fire regimes. To answer this question, we developed the Landscape Dynamics Simulator (LADS) to simulate wildfires and the dynamics of old-growth forests in historical landscapes ([Wimberly et al. 2000](#western-refs), [Wimberly 2002](#western-refs)). Despite the occurrence of large wildfires, we found that old growth was historically the most prevalent age class, covering 29-52% of the total forest area. The current area of old-growth forest is considerably lower than this historical range of variability ([Wimberly et al. 2004](#western-refs)). More recent versions of LADS have been modified to better model the dynamics of mixed-severity fire regimes ([Wimberly and Kennedy 2008](#western-refs), [Kennedy and Wimberly 2009](#western-refs)). In the future, a warmer and drier climate will result in increased fire frequencies and severities that will push landscapes even further outside the range of historical variability ([Wimberly and Liu 2014](#western-refs)).
